title: From promises to proof: Why outcomes are the new currency of development cooperation
gist: As EU official development assistance fell nearly 10% in real terms in 2025, a World Bank Group official argues that budget cuts and public skepticism now form a reinforcing 'scarcity-skepticism' cycle, and that rebuilding political support for aid requires fewer but sharper outcome indicators tracked during delivery (not just at project end) plus candid transparency about failures.

insights.claim: Official development assistance from EU donor countries fell by nearly 10 percent in real terms in 2025 according to the OECD, even as a G7 survey by AFD-IFOP found three-quarters of people still support aid to developing countries, while almost half also agreed international cooperation could be a waste of public money.
insights.speaker: Lisandro Martin
insights.so_what: Public support for aid has not collapsed, but conditional skepticism has -- a distinction that should shift aid-agency strategy from defending the concept of aid to proving its results.
insights.locator: In 2025, official development assistance from European Union donor countries fell

insights.claim: In the same G7 survey, 81 percent of respondents said knowing how aid money is used would strengthen their support, and 79 percent wanted to see concrete results on the ground -- indicating public backing for aid is now conditional on demonstrated outcomes rather than unconditional.
insights.speaker: Lisandro Martin
insights.so_what: A specific, quantified public mandate (81% want transparency, 79% want results) that donor agencies and multilaterals can point to when justifying investment in outcome-tracking and reporting infrastructure.
insights.quote: 81 percent said that knowing how the money is used would strengthen their support, while 79 percent wanted to see concrete results on the ground
insights.locator: A few months later, an AFD-IFOP survey found

insights.claim: Budget cuts and public skepticism reinforce each other in a compounding cycle: cuts erode the scale and continuity needed to deliver visible outcomes, weak delivery appears to confirm skepticism, and that skepticism weakens the political constituency for aid, making the next round of cuts easier to justify.
insights.speaker: Lisandro Martin
insights.so_what: A reusable causal model (scarcity initiates, skepticism multiplies) for understanding why aid-budget declines can accelerate rather than plateau once public trust erodes -- relevant to forecasting further ODA cuts across donor countries.
insights.quote: Scarcity may initiate the cycle. Skepticism is what multiplies it.
insights.locator: A budget cut subtracts. Skepticism compounds.

themes.theme: Fewer, sharper indicators over more metrics

insights.claim: The World Bank Group's Mid-Term Review of its institutional Scorecard is being framed not as a technical exercise but as a 'confidence contract' with governments, partners, and citizens, built around focusing on fewer, clearer outcome indicators rather than adding more measures.
insights.speaker: Lisandro Martin
insights.so_what: Runs counter to the instinct that more accountability requires more metrics; argues excess indicator complexity in an anxious environment can itself look like evasion.
insights.quote: in an anxious environment, complexity can look like evasion

insights.claim: Outcomes should be measured during project delivery, not only at the end, so that evidence can show in real time where progress is accelerating or falling short and where resources or partnerships need to change while there is still time to act.
insights.speaker: Lisandro Martin
insights.so_what: A mid-delivery monitoring approach is a template applicable beyond the World Bank to any large multi-year program facing scrutiny over results and course-correction capacity.
insights.locator: It also requires measurement during delivery

insights.claim: Concrete illustrative outcomes cited include: in Malawi, electricity expansion measured by businesses staying open, clinics improving service, and students studying at night; in Senegal, The Gambia, and Guinea, agricultural support measured by higher farmer incomes and more jobs; and in the Democratic Republic of Congo, road rehabilitation measured by improved access to markets, schools, and health services.
insights.speaker: Lisandro Martin
insights.so_what: Concrete country examples of the World Bank's shift toward outcome-based (versus output-based) program evaluation across Africa.
insights.locator: Across Africa, the test is concrete
